summary:
Delta State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies in the state, as does section 217 of the Criminal Code, which makes male gross indecency a felony carrying three years' imprisonment; the maximum exposure under the 2014 Act is 14 years' imprisonment. Delta has enacted no protective statute of its own. The death penalty attached to same-sex conduct under Shari'a provisions operates only in the twelve northern states and has no application in Delta.

Enforcement in Delta has taken the form of raids on private hotel gatherings. In June 2018 police in Asaba arrested more than 100 people attending a party at a hotel on charges that they were gay and lesbian, and by July 2018 the group was facing homosexuality-related charges in court.

The Warri raid of 27 August 2023 is the most detailed Delta incident in this inventory. At around 9 pm, officers from the Ekpan Division of the Delta State Police Command raided Teebolus Hotel on Refinery Road, Ekpan, in Uvwie Local Government Area and arrested 67 people at what police described as a same-sex wedding between a 22-year-old groom and a 20-year-old bride. The command spokesman, DSP Bright Edafe, said the operation followed a confession by a male cross-dresser that he belonged to a gay club travelling to a marriage ceremony, that the suspects fled on the officers' arrival, that 67 were chased and arrested, and that drugs and 'gay marriage ceremonial dresses' were recovered. The 67, publicly known as the 'Warri 67', were charged to court, and the spokesman said efforts continued to arrest those who fled.

Accounts of that night differ. The USSD 2023 human rights report records that police raided a 'white party' organised by the LGBTQI+ community in Delta State on 27 August 2023 and detained more than 200 individuals, that police alleged the event was a same-sex wedding, and that some civil society representatives disputed that description. One of the 67 arrested at the Warri hotel alleged that he was sexually assaulted by a man at the hotel while intoxicated.

Reporting from Delta indicates that the law suppresses complaints as well as enabling arrests. A human rights lawyer based in Warri told the UK Home Office that victims of 'kito' — predatory same-sex assault and extortion — under-report for fear of prosecution under the same statute. A visitor who uses dating or hook-up applications in the state faces the same luring and blackmail pattern documented nationally, in which the threat of disclosure is the leverage.
tangentialFactors:
Delta's documented enforcement consists of two mass arrests on single nights, in June 2018 at Asaba and on 27 August 2023 at Warri. These are raw arrest totals from individual operations, not incidence rates, and no per-capita or population comparison is available for the state; they should not be read as a measure of how often such operations occur.

The two accounts of the August 2023 operation differ in scale and in characterisation: 67 people charged after an alleged same-sex wedding, against more than 200 detained at an event described by organisers as a 'white party'. The discrepancy is unresolved in the sources, and the police framing of the event is contested by civil society representatives cited in the same reporting.

Charges in Delta have been framed alongside drug allegations and, in the police account, alongside a cross-dresser's confession about a gay club. Gender presentation and association, not conduct alone, are stated triggers for the operation.

The most recent Delta incident in this inventory is dated 27 August 2023. No later Delta-specific arrest, prosecution or violence incident is documented here, and the absence of later records is not evidence that such operations have stopped.
localsOnly:
The 67 people arrested at the Warri hotel on 27 August 2023 were charged to court, and the Delta State Police Command stated at the time that suspects and exhibits were in custody and that efforts to arrest fleeing members for possible prosecution were continuing. The group arrested at Asaba in June 2018 was facing homosexuality-related charges in court by July 2018. No outcome, dismissal or conviction in either case is recorded in this inventory.

Residents of Delta have no state-level protective statute to rely on. A human rights lawyer practising in Warri reported that victims of 'kito' assault and extortion do not report to police because reporting risks prosecution under the same anti-LGBT framework, which leaves the extortionists' leverage intact.

Delta State Police Command publicity around the Warri operation named the alleged ceremony, the recovered items and the cross-dresser's confession, indicating that the state's own account of the raid is a matter of public record and that suspects' identities were circulated through official channels.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the Warri 67 prosecutions and the Asaba prosecutions have concluded, and with what result. The inventory records the charges and no disposition.

Unresolved: whether the 67 people charged and the more than 200 individuals detained are the same operation counted differently, or two separate actions on 27 August 2023. Both sources give that date; the counts and the description of the event do not match.

Unresolved: whether the sexual assault alleged by one of the Warri detainees was investigated by any authority. The allegation appears in police-related reporting and no follow-up is documented.

Unresolved: whether Delta State has any policy on the custody placement of transgender detainees, on document or marker rules, or on access to gender-related healthcare. No state-level instrument on any of these is present in the inventory, and none should be assumed either way.

State-level documentation for Delta is limited to these incidents. The inventory contains no survey of trans residents of Delta, no count of violence against trans people in the state, and no figure that could be compared with a general crime rate. Thin documentation does not demonstrate safety.
